text: A man comes home to the town that raised him and finds he can no longer speak its dialect. Abdallah is in Nouadhibou, on the Mauritanian coast, waiting out the last weeks before he leaves for the West, and his western clothes settle the question of who he is before he opens his mouth. Sissako gives ninety-one minutes to that interval and spends almost none of them on the decision itself. A boy runs errands. An elderly electrician goes on stringing light. What accumulates is a tally of what will not survive the crossing, kept by someone who has already half departed and lacks the words to say so to anyone still there. The film carries the Étalon d'Or de Yennenga and a place on the Guardian's hundred best films of the twenty-first century, which is an odd destiny for something pitched this low.

Everyone the thief came up with has moved into trades with proper names, and he is still working with his hands in other people's pockets. That is the whole situation, and Jia Zhangke lets it run a hundred and thirteen minutes. The small town around him is not a backdrop so much as a set of new rules arriving faster than one man can learn them, and the film is unsentimental about him without ever being cruel. It watches someone go on practising a skill the people nearest him have quietly agreed to stop needing. What comes of that is closer to grief than to defiance: not a man refusing to change, but a man who was never offered terms he could meet. The Golden Horse hundred and a New Currents award came later. The bitterness arrived first, in 1997.

Everything here is built to be looked at, which is a defensible reading of a novel about money that exists to be seen. Nick Carraway arrives from the Midwest, lands next door to Jay Gatsby on Long Island, and is drawn into a world he can describe far better than he can join. Luhrmann takes a hundred and forty-three minutes and spends them on surfaces — houses, clothes, volume — refusing the hush that usually settles over Fitzgerald on screen. The film collected AACTA prizes for its leading and supporting performances and for best film, and IndieWire counted it among the decade's best. Its argument is unfashionable and fairly simple: the nouveau riche existence at the centre was always a performance, and filming a performance as a performance is closer to accuracy than to vulgarity.

A building coming apart, and inside it doors that open not onto other rooms but onto memory, dream, and the parts of both that go wrong. Jozef has come to visit his father; that errand is the last ordinary thing in the film, since the sanatorium's layout turns out to be made of his own head, which makes walking through a door the main event. Wojciech Has takes a hundred and twenty-four minutes and shows no interest in explaining the rules. He works by density instead — images arriving faster than they can be sorted, dream logic followed without hesitation, horror that never announces itself as a genre. Poland in 1973, with no reliable clock and almost no exterior plot. A Jury Prize and a standing place among the best Polish films are the record; the film itself is closer to being inside weather.

Eight is an oddly specific number of demons, and someone in the story did the counting. A priest arrives at a convent to save its Mother Superior from possession, and the meeting of those two — the only people in the building whose profession is God — is the whole of the drama. Kawalerowicz keeps it to a hundred and six minutes and to a very small world: a religious house, a few rooms, a task no amount of force will finish. It holds a Jury Prize and a permanent place on the Polish list, though its standing is not what makes it hold. The film is filed as horror and earns the label, but the fear in it is procedural as much as supernatural, and it presses hardest on what a vocation costs the person carrying one when faith and appetite are kept behind the same walls.

The chase is the subject here; the case that started it is a formality. Detective Woo is after a gangster called Sungmin who can change his face as easily as a coat, and Lee Myung-se builds a hundred and eight minutes around the pursuit itself. A man who can be anyone is not a mystery to be solved but a problem of stamina — nobody deduces their way to him, they can only outlast him — so the film organizes itself as movement, repetition and accumulating fatigue. The trail runs out at the edge of a coal-mining town, a setting with no glamour to lend anyone. Blue Dragon named it best film and it sits on the KOFA hundred. What it offers is not suspense but momentum, sustained well past the point where most thrillers stop to explain themselves.

In 1990 a film about a fugitive chose to spend its hundred minutes on his shift work rather than his politics. The student activist in Park Kwang-su's drama is hiding from the authorities in a small mining town, so his convictions live in his pocket while he labours beside people whose position was never a matter of conviction at all. Hiding is usually a plot device. Here it has hours and wages attached, and the pressure comes as much from that imbalance as from any risk of being found: an educated outsider dependent on the discretion of a town that owes him nothing. The distance between believing in workers and living among them is the thing under examination. Blue Dragon gave it best film and it holds a place on the KOFA hundred, a record that suits a work assembled out of shifts, rooms and the arithmetic of not being noticed.

Most of the men are gone from the valley; the work they did is not. The Korean War has stripped a mountain village down to women and labour, and Kim Soo-yong needs only eighty minutes to establish that what remains is an economy of secrets — who is spoken about, who is not, who knows and stays quiet. A widow finds a guerrilla hiding in a bamboo grove and does not report him. That is the whole hinge, and it is enough, because the risk belongs to everyone within earshot rather than to the two of them alone. The film is short and unhurried, a combination that usually means the pressure comes from somewhere other than plot. Here it comes from proximity: a grove close enough to the houses that concealment can only ever be temporary, and a hunger the war did not create but did leave unattended.

An ice storm is a poor metaphor and an excellent inconvenience: it strands people who were already working hard at avoiding each other. The weekend after Thanksgiving, 1973, and the Hood family is skidding in the way of households where everyone has private business to conduct. Then the worst storm in a century settles over all of it. Ang Lee's method is coolness rather than irony; the parents get the same seriousness as the teenagers, which is rarer than it sounds, and the period is allowed to furnish itself instead of performing the seventies. It sits on the They Shoot Pictures Don't They? thousand and holds a screenplay prize. A hundred and thirteen minutes, one long weekend, nobody exempt and nobody blamed — which is why the discomfort is so hard to put down afterwards.

Two young men who run for a living get sent to the Ottoman Empire. Peter Weir gives a long early stretch of his hundred and twelve minutes to the running itself — training, rivalry, distance covered for no reason beyond the covering of it — so that enlistment arrives as one more thing worth being quick for. The film took awards for two of its performances and for its cinematography, along with a best film prize and a place in a National Board of Review top ten, and the photography is doing work rather than decorating: sunlight, space, and bodies moving through both. The proportions are what make it unusual. Most war pictures treat the time before as preamble; this one treats it as the substance, and lets the campaign in the title sit at the far end like a fact everyone already knows and nobody is hurrying toward.

The escape happens early; almost everything after it is walking, and the film knows that is the harder subject. In 1931 three Aboriginal girls are taken from their families to be trained as domestic staff, and the Outback that follows is filmed by Phillip Noyce less as landscape than as an amount — something counted in days and in feet rather than admired from a height. Ninety-four minutes is short for a journey that long, which forces a choice: either explain the policy that produced these children's situation, or follow them. It follows them. The adapted screenplay, the cinematography and a supporting performance were all recognized, and the film took a best film award and a National Board of Review top-ten place. What stays is the arithmetic — small people, adult pursuers, and ground indifferent to which is right.

A boy is happy where he is, and his happiness is precisely what is at stake. PS lives in suburban Sydney with his aunt Lila and her husband George on very little money, and he is content there, until Lila's wealthy sister Vanessa comes back from England and takes an interest in him. Carl Schultz films the ensuing struggle from inside the child, where adult motives are large, unreadable and conducted just out of hearing. Three acting awards followed, which figures: the drama sits almost entirely in what grown-ups say in front of a boy, and in the small adjustments they make on remembering he is there. A hundred and ten minutes, one household set against another, money on one side of it, and a running argument carried on in tones a child is not meant to decode.

Sixty-eight minutes: barely a feature, and the thrift shows in every decision. A boxer whose career is finishing falls for a dancer whose employer is violent, and the film discharges those obligations briskly, as though the story were a fee paid for permission to photograph New York City at night. That is where the interest sits — the corners of the city the plot gives it an excuse to visit, squalor attended to more carefully than the dialogue ever is. Kubrick was working cheap, and the constraint is legible; it also suits a picture about people with no margin. It carries a Golden Leopard. What holds is not the abduction plot but the walking: a man crossing a city that has already worked out how little it owes him.

Ten strangers accept an invitation from a host who never appears, and then a recording tells each of them what they have done. René Clair spends ninety-eight minutes running that machine, and much of the pleasure is mechanical: a closed island, a fixed cast, a rule everyone can state and nobody can leave. The setup is a puzzle, but the interesting pressure is social. These are people who arrived as guests and must go on being guests, holding manners in place well past the point where manners help, while the arithmetic of the room quietly worsens. Accusation before evidence, suspicion before proof, and a house in which politeness is the last remaining protocol. It carries a Golden Leopard. A film built almost entirely out of rooms and reasoning, and it never needs more than that.
